```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

The package fits regression models with skew-normal errors,
$$
y_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\beta + \varepsilon_i,\qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim \mathrm{SN}(0, \sigma, \alpha),
$$
and a partially linear version in which one covariate enters through a
penalized B-spline. Four estimators are available: maximum likelihood, the
corrective estimator that subtracts the Cox and Snell second-order bias, and
the mean and median bias-reducing adjusted score estimators.

```{r}
library(snbr)
```

## The Arctic lake data

The data set `arcticlake` gives the sand, silt and clay proportions of 39
sediment samples taken at different depths of an Arctic lake. We model the
logit of the clay proportion as a quadratic function of depth, with depth
expressed in hundreds of metres.

```{r}
arcticlake$d <- arcticlake$depth / 100
fit_ml <- snreg(logit_clay ~ d + I(d^2), data = arcticlake, method = "ML")
fit_ml
```

The maximum likelihood estimate of the shape is minus infinity. The decision
is exact: `sn_mle()` compares the best finite value of the log-likelihood
with its limit as $\alpha \to \pm\infty$, which is the log-likelihood of a
half-normal regression fitted by constrained least squares.

```{r}
f <- sn_mle(cbind(1, arcticlake$d, arcticlake$d^2), arcticlake$logit_clay)
f$loglik_limit   # limits as alpha -> -Inf and alpha -> +Inf
f$finite
```

The corrective estimator needs a finite maximum likelihood estimate and is
therefore not available. The adjusted score estimators are:

```{r}
fit_mean <- snreg(logit_clay ~ d + I(d^2), data = arcticlake, method = "mean")
fit_med  <- snreg(logit_clay ~ d + I(d^2), data = arcticlake, method = "median")
cbind(mean = coef(fit_mean), median = coef(fit_med))
summary(fit_mean)
```

## A smooth effect of depth

The quadratic was chosen by the authors of the earlier analysis among a few
alternatives. A penalized spline lets the data decide; the smoothing
parameter is chosen by AIC with effective degrees of freedom.

```{r}
fit_s <- snreg(logit_clay ~ 1, data = arcticlake, smooth = "d", method = "mean", k = 8)
fit_s
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Logit of clay proportion against depth with the fitted location and mean curves."}
th <- coef(fit_s)
P <- length(th)
delta <- th[P] / sqrt(1 + th[P]^2)
loc <- fitted(fit_s)
avg <- loc + th[P - 1] * sqrt(2 / pi) * delta   # E(y) = location + sigma * b * delta
o <- order(arcticlake$d)
plot(arcticlake$depth, arcticlake$logit_clay, pch = 19, col = "grey40",
     ylim = range(c(arcticlake$logit_clay, loc)),
     xlab = "depth (m)", ylab = "logit(clay)")
lines(arcticlake$depth[o], loc[o], lwd = 2, col = "#14365d")
lines(arcticlake$depth[o], avg[o], lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "#e8a33d")
legend("bottomright", c("location", "mean"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2),
       col = c("#14365d", "#e8a33d"), bty = "n")
```

The solid line is the location $\mathbf{x}_i^\top\beta + f(t_i)$ and
the dashed line the mean. With a negative shape the errors are skewed to the
left, so the location lies above the bulk of the data and the mean below it.

## Second-order bias

`sn_bias()` evaluates the Cox and Snell bias at any parameter value; it is
the ingredient of both the corrective and the mean bias-reducing estimators.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
X <- cbind(1, runif(50))
sn_bias(c(-2, 2, 1, 5), X)
```
